tldr: This paper combines closed-form variable-curvature kinematics with a multipoint CBF-QP for multi-segment tendon-driven continuum robots with spatially varying cross-sections and stiffness, achieving both whole-body collision avoidance and millisecond-level real-time control.

(B) Whole-body multipoint obstacle avoidance using monitoring points along the backbone. (C) CBF-QP control loop that tracks nominal tip velocity while optimizing under safety constraints.
overview:
Slender and flexible tendon-driven continuum robots (TDCRs) hold great promise for exploration in confined spaces and medical applications. However, two major hurdles have hindered practical deployment. First, when stiffness or tendon spacing varies along the robot's length, conventional piecewise constant curvature (PCC) models fail to accurately predict the shape. Conversely, solving rigorous models like Cosserat rod theory requires numerical computation of boundary value problems, making real-time control difficult. Second, ensuring safety across the entire slender body is challenging. Since the entire body—not just the tip—risks contacting the environment, whole-body collision avoidance is essential, but guaranteeing safety for high-degree-of-freedom flexible bodies in real time has been tough.

To solve this, the authors devised a unified control framework operating purely in actuation space (tendon displacement space). First, based on the principle of minimum potential energy, they developed variable-curvature kinematics that analytically derive the curvature distribution and whole-body Jacobians in closed form, even for structures with continuously varying stiffness and tendon spacing. Furthermore, they placed numerous safety monitoring points along the backbone, designed control barrier functions (CBFs) that handle dynamic obstacles, and formulated the problem as a quadratic program (QP). A key highlight is that the decision dimension of the QP depends only on the number of independently actuated segments (just 3 dimensions in this study), rather than the number of monitoring points.

Validated in MuJoCo physics simulations, the proposed method achieved high collision-free success rates of 96% in static obstacle scenarios and 100% in dynamic obstacle scenarios (compared to approximately 60% and 80% without CBF constraints). Moreover, even with a dense grid of 600 monitoring points along the backbone, the mean computation time per control step was only 6.66 ms, demonstrating impressive real-time performance.
contributions: Derived closed-form variable-curvature forward and inverse kinematics as well as analytical Jacobians based on the principle of minimum potential energy for continuum robots with spatially varying stiffness and tendon spacing
Proposed a multipoint CBF-QP safety filter that guarantees clearance margins across the entire backbone while accounting for dynamic obstacle velocities and actuation velocity bounds

Demonstrated high scalability by restricting the QP decision variable dimension solely to the number of independently actuated segments, achieving a 6.66 ms control period even with 600 safety monitoring points on the backbone
Demonstrated high collision avoidance performance across 100 statistical evaluation trials in the MuJoCo physics simulator for static and dynamic obstacle avoidance as well as hole-traversal tasks

sections.heading: The Dilemma of Accuracy vs. Whole-Body Safety in Real-Time Continuum Robot Control
sections.summary: Slender, flexible tendon-driven continuum robots excel in confined spaces, but handling their complex nonuniform deformation and whole-body collision risks in real time has long been a challenge. Existing constant-curvature models lack accuracy, while rigorous mechanics models and trajectory planners are computationally too heavy. This study breaks through this dilemma by integrating a closed-form variable-curvature model with a multipoint CBF-QP.
sections.details:
Continuum robots possess high adaptability to smoothly enter narrow environments because their flexible core, called the backbone, bends continuously. In particular, tendon-driven continuum robots (TDCRs), which place actuators (such as motors) at the base and bend segments via tendons, are gaining attention because they keep the body slender while independently driving multiple segments.

However, when attempting real-time motion control in confined or dynamic spaces, two major hurdles arise.
- **Modeling Nonuniform Deformation**: Robot stiffness, cross-sectional dimensions, and tendon routing intervals often vary along the backbone to reduce weight or tailor performance. Yet, widely used piecewise constant curvature (PCC) models assume each segment is a constant circular arc, leading to large shape prediction errors. On the other hand, solving continuum mechanics models like Euler-Bernoulli beam or Cosserat rod equations requires solving boundary value problems, which is computationally prohibitive inside a high-frequency control loop.
- **Whole-Body Collision Avoidance**: Because the robot is slender, guiding only the tip safely can still leave the intermediate body (backbone) crashing into obstacles. Sampling-based planners and nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) take too long to compute, while reactive local avoidance methods lack forward invariance guarantees (the mathematical assurance of never leaving the safe set).

Against this backdrop, this paper focuses on Control Barrier Functions (CBFs). CBFs can translate safety conditions into affine constraints on the control input, acting as a "safety filter" that minimally modifies a nominal input via a quadratic program (QP). In this work, the authors build a closed-form variable-curvature kinematic model that captures structural nonuniformities, using its analytical Jacobians to propose a multipoint CBF-QP safety control framework running on millisecond scales.

sections.heading: Unlocking Nonuniform Continuum Mechanics with Energy Principles: Closed-Form Kinematics
sections.summary: The relationship between tendon displacements and continuous curvature variation is formulated as an elastic strain energy minimization problem under geometric constraints. Using Lagrange multipliers, the local curvature, tangent angles, Cartesian coordinates, and point Jacobians at any arbitrary location are all derived in closed form (analytically) for multi-segment robots with nonuniform cross-sections and stiffness.
sections.details:
This section builds the kinematics of an $n$-segment planar TDCR based on actuation space (the tendon displacement vector $\Delta \boldsymbol{L}$).

### II-A Geometric Relations and Energy Functional
Let the arc-length coordinate along the backbone be $s \in [0, L]$ and the tangent angle be $\theta(s,t)$; the local curvature is then expressed as $\kappa_i(s,t) = \theta_i'(s,t)$. Between the length variation $\Delta L_i$ of symmetrically routed tendons and the local curvature, a geometric integral relation holds via the local tendon spacing $W_i(s)$. Additionally, the elastic strain energy resulting from backbone bending deformation is expressed using the segment-wise bending stiffness $E_i I_i(s)$. The equilibrium shape is formulated as a variational problem that minimizes elastic strain energy while satisfying the geometric tendon displacement constraints.

### II-B Variable-Curvature Forward Kinematic Mapping
To solve this constrained variational problem, a time-dependent Lagrange multiplier $\lambda_i(t)$ is introduced for each segment. Applying the variational principle (stationarity conditions) and resolving geometric continuity of tangent angles across segments alongside base and tip boundary conditions, the local curvature field $\kappa_i(s,t)$ emerges in a remarkably simple closed form:
$$\kappa_i(s,t) = \frac{2 q_i(t)}{\Gamma_i} \frac{W_i(s)}{E_i I_i(s)}$$
Here, $q_i(t) = \Delta L_i(t)$, and $\Gamma_i$ is an actuation compliance coefficient determined by segment geometry and material properties. In other words, local curvature is completely determined by the given tendon displacement and the ratio of local tendon spacing to bending stiffness. Integrating this along the arc length yields the tangent angle $\theta(s,t)$ and Cartesian position $\boldsymbol{p}(s,t)$ from the base to any location $s$ in closed form, completing the forward kinematics.

### II-C Residual-Based Variable-Curvature Inverse Kinematics
Next, inverse kinematics and differential kinematics are considered. An analytical point Jacobian $\boldsymbol{J}(s,t) \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times n}$ connecting Cartesian velocity at any arc length $s$ with tendon velocity $\Delta \dot{\boldsymbol{L}}$ is derived. For the tip position $\boldsymbol{p}_e$, a first-order asymptotically stable dynamic $\dot{\boldsymbol{e}}_p + k \boldsymbol{e}_p = \boldsymbol{0}$ is imposed on the tracking residual $\boldsymbol{e}_p$ relative to the desired trajectory $\boldsymbol{p}_d$. When the segment count $n > 2$, the robot is redundant for planar tasks, so the nominal actuation velocity $\boldsymbol{u}_{\mathrm{nom}}(t)$ is computed using the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse (or damped least-squares near singularities).

sections.heading: Enveloping the Entire Body Safely: Real-Time Safety Filters via Multipoint CBFs and Low-Dimensional QPs
sections.summary: Using distances between numerous monitoring points along the backbone and multiple obstacles, inequality constraints are constructed via control barrier functions (CBFs) to guarantee forward invariance of the safe set. A quadratic program (QP) minimally modifies the nominal tip-tracking inputs; because the decision variable dimension is strictly $n$ (the segment count), it solves extremely quickly.
sections.details:
A safety control algorithm is designed to protect the entire flexible body, not just the tip.

### III-A Actuation-Space System and Whole-Body Safe Set
The robot's actuation state is defined as $\boldsymbol{q}(t) = \Delta \boldsymbol{L}(t)$, and the control input as the tendon velocity $\boldsymbol{u}(t) = \dot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t)$. Along the robot's backbone, $N_\alpha$ safety monitoring points $s_k$ are distributed. When $N_o$ obstacles (with positions $\boldsymbol{p}_o$ and velocities $\dot{\boldsymbol{p}}_o$) exist in the environment, a safety function $h_{k,o} = \|\boldsymbol{p}_k - \boldsymbol{p}_o\|^2 - d_o^2 \ge 0$ is defined for each monitoring point and obstacle pair using an allowable clearance margin $d_o$. The set where $h_{k,o} \ge 0$ holds across all pairs defines the robot's "whole-body safe set."

### III-B Multipoint Control Barrier Function Constraints
To ensure the robot does not leave this safe set (maintaining forward invariance), a first-order CBF condition $\dot{h}_{k,o} + \gamma h_{k,o} \ge 0$ (gain $\gamma > 0$) is enforced. Expanding the time derivative introduces the monitoring point's Cartesian velocity $\dot{\boldsymbol{p}}_k = \boldsymbol{J}_k \boldsymbol{u}$ and the obstacle velocity $\dot{\boldsymbol{p}}_o$. Rearranging yields an affine inequality constraint on the control input $\boldsymbol{u}(t)$: $\boldsymbol{A}_{k,o}(t) \boldsymbol{u}(t) \ge b_{k,o}(t)$. By vertically stacking all $N_\alpha \times N_o$ constraints, the whole-body safety requirement is unified into the matrix form $\boldsymbol{A}_h(t) \boldsymbol{u}(t) \ge \boldsymbol{b}_h(t)$.

### III-C Real-Time Whole-Body Safe Motion Control via CBF-QP
The core controller is formulated as a quadratic program (QP) that minimally adjusts the nominal input $\boldsymbol{u}_{\mathrm{nom}}(t)$ from inverse kinematics while respecting safety constraints and actuator velocity bounds $[\boldsymbol{u}_{\min}, \boldsymbol{u}_{\max}]$:
$$\min_{\boldsymbol{u} \in \mathbb{R}^n} \frac{1}{2} \|\boldsymbol{u} - \boldsymbol{u}_{\mathrm{nom}}\|^2 \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \boldsymbol{A}_h \boldsymbol{u} \ge \boldsymbol{b}_h, \quad \boldsymbol{u}_{\min} \le \boldsymbol{u} \le \boldsymbol{u}_{\max}$$
The standout feature here is that regardless of how many monitoring points are added or how many constraint rows accumulate, **the optimization decision variable $\boldsymbol{u}$ remains of dimension $n$, matching only the segment count**. This enables dense whole-body safety monitoring while running the safety filter continuously at millisecond loop rates.

sections.heading: Simulation Results: Shape Accuracy, High-Density Monitoring, and Flawless Dynamic Obstacle Avoidance
sections.summary: The accuracy of the variable-curvature model is validated against rigorous Cosserat beam reference solutions (GVS), followed by static, dynamic, and hole-traversal tests inside the MuJoCo physics simulator. The proposed method achieves collision-free success rates of 96% (static) and 100% (dynamic), with an average computation time of only 6.66 ms even with 600 monitoring points.
sections.details:
The performance of the proposed kinematic model and CBF-QP controller is evaluated from multiple angles through simulations.

### IV-A Simulation Setup
A 3-segment TDCR (lengths $0.30\,\mathrm{m}, 0.25\,\mathrm{m}, 0.20\,\mathrm{m}$, total length $0.75\,\mathrm{m}$) was used for validation. Tendon routing intervals vary non-uniformly across segments at $16.5\,\mathrm{mm}, 23.5\,\mathrm{mm}, 30.5\,\mathrm{mm}$. As a kinematic reference, an accurate geometric variable strain (GVS) approach solving Cosserat rod equations was adopted. Furthermore, a Sim-to-Sim environment using the MuJoCo physics simulator was built to evaluate control performance under contact dynamics with rigid obstacles.

### IV-B 1 Variable-Curvature Model Accuracy
Comparing backbone shapes between the proposed model and GVS over a 20-second trajectory revealed close agreement. The maximum absolute curvature errors for each segment from base to tip were tightly bounded at $2.109 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}$, $4.929 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}$, and $5.223 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}$, proving that complex bending caused by structural nonuniformity can be captured accurately by the closed-form model.

### IV-B 2 Whole-Body Collision Avoidance
Across 100 independent trials for each scenario in MuJoCo:
- **Static Obstacle Environment**: The proposed method achieved a 96% collision-free success rate. The 4% failure cases were due to the robot getting surrounded by obstacles, where conservative CBF constraints trapped it in local minima. In contrast, the baseline without CBFs achieved only about 60% success because the body caught on obstacles and locked up.
- **Dynamic Obstacle Environment**: When obstacles moved toward the robot, the proposed method avoided collisions in all 100 trials (100% success rate), compared to about 80% for the baseline.
- **Hole-Traversal Task**: In a task requiring the robot to pass through a narrow wall aperture, it traversed smoothly without rubbing its body.

### IV-B 3 Computation Time Evaluation
Computation times were measured across different monitoring point sampling densities. Even when increasing the monitoring points along the backbone to 600 (a dense spacing of roughly $1.25\,\mathrm{mm}$), the mean computation time per control step was only $6.66\,\mathrm{ms}$. This demonstrates that whole-body safety monitoring can comfortably run in high-frequency control loops around 150 Hz, strongly verifying the framework's real-time capability and scalability.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Next Steps: Moving to Hardware and Even Tighter Environments
sections.summary: A unified framework combining closed-form variable-curvature kinematics with a low-dimensional CBF-QP was established for continuum robots with nonuniform structures. Achieving 96% static and 100% dynamic collision avoidance alongside 6.66 ms fast computation, future work will focus on hardware validation and improving escape strategies in tightly constrained spaces.
sections.details:
This paper presented a real-time whole-body safe motion generation framework operating entirely in actuation space for planar multi-segment TDCRs.

Its key strength lies in the elegant coupling between the closed-form variable-curvature model based on minimum potential energy and the multipoint CBF-QP whose decision dimension depends solely on the number of actuated segments. This allows accurate compensation for nonuniform structural parameters while executing whole-body collision avoidance within milliseconds, even with hundreds of monitoring points along the backbone.

For future work, the authors point to experimental validation on physical hardware. They also aim to introduce deadlock-resolution strategies and integration with high-level task planners to overcome cases where conservative CBF constraints temporarily stall the robot in extremely narrow corridors.

takeaways: Even for continuum robots with nonuniform stiffness and tendon spacing, curvature and Jacobians can be determined in closed form (analytically) using the minimum potential energy principle and Lagrange multipliers.

In continuum whole-body safe control, defining the QP decision variables in segment actuation space rather than task space or monitoring point space allows millisecond-order solutions even with hundreds of monitoring points.
Formulating first-order CBFs that incorporate obstacle velocity terms guarantees high collision avoidance rates (100% in this paper) even when dynamic obstacles approach the robot.
limitations: Validation is currently limited to planar (2D) motion and simulation (MuJoCo); extending to 3D space and handling real-world friction and hysteresis remain future work.
Local safety constraints from CBFs can introduce conservatism, causing the robot to occasionally stall (get trapped in local minima) when surrounded by tight obstacles.
Because the backbone is monitored at discrete points, strict safety guarantees against tiny obstacles or sharp corners that might slip between monitoring points depend on sampling density.
